But do you know where that version came from?

Hindu stories often live across texts, regions and centuries of retelling. Details can change — sometimes significantly.

At Sandhya Katha, we show the source and locus we used, and when traditions differ, we say so rather than blending them into one convenient version.

We are not trying to decide which tradition is “right.”

We want parents to know what they are telling their children — and where it comes from.

The story matters. The source matters too.

The honest answer is that the sources do not all line up the same way.

In the Skanda Purāṇa, Gaṇeśa is called Kumāraguru — “the elder brother of Kumāra.”

In the Śiva Purāṇa’s Śvetakalpa birth narrative, the six-faced Kumāra is already present during the battle surrounding the newly born Gaṇeśa. And that same Śiva Purāṇa explicitly says Gaṇeśa’s birth story is told differently across kalpas.

That is not something Sandhya Katha wants to quietly smooth over.

We name the source. We give the passage. And when tellings differ, we say so — without deciding that one living tradition is the “wrong” one.

The old stories deserve their addresses.

Gaṇeśa Chaturthi is almost here. 🌙🐘🙏🛕

Who is older: Gaṇeśa or Kārttikeya?

The honest answer is that the sources do not all line up the same way.

In the Skanda Purāṇa, Gaṇeśa is called Kumāraguru — “the elder brother of Kumāra.”

In the Śiva Purāṇa’s Śvetakalpa birth narrative, the six-faced Kumāra is already present during the battle surrounding the newly born Gaṇeśa. And that same Śiva Purāṇa explicitly says Gaṇeśa’s birth story is told differently across kalpas.

That is not something Sandhya Katha wants to quietly smooth over.

We name the source. We give the passage. And when tellings differ, we say so — without deciding that one living tradition is the “wrong” one.

The old stories deserve their addresses.

Tonight, light a lamp.

Just the old stories, carefully brought back to the evening.
